trade: Science class with the tidal restoration crew at a slough — learner and restoration crew lead
header: Lower-secondary science at the Yosemite Slough Restoration Site in San Francisco: how tides carry mud into a marsh and drop it where the water slows, why a marsh needs that mud to keep up with the water, tested in a tide tray and seen on the crew's mats, using only what the tray and the slough in the scene show.
name: Mud on the Move
tagline: Tides carry mud in and drop it where water slows — test it in a tray, then see why marshes need it

badge.name: Mud Mover
badge.note: Showed in a tide tray where moving water drops its mud, explained why a marsh needs that mud and watched the crew work from mats

hazards.label: Say the mud in the water is dirt to get rid of?
hazards.text: You said the mud in the water is dirt to get rid of. Marshes are built from that mud. Each tide leaves a thin layer, and over time the layers raise the marsh so it can keep up with the water.

hazards.label: Walk out onto the soft mud at low tide?
hazards.text: You started out onto the soft mud. Tidal mud can hold a boot fast, and the tide comes back in. The crew works from wide mats and boardwalks, and visitors stay on the firm path.

hazards.label: Make the water faster and add more mud in the same run?
hazards.text: You changed the water speed and the amount of mud in the same run. With two changes you cannot tell which one made the difference. Change one thing, the speed, and keep the mud the same.

hazards.label: Ignore the crew's tide board?
hazards.text: You skipped the tide board. The crew plans every job around the tide, because rising water changes where it is safe to stand. Read the board first, like the crew does.

find1.title: Find where the water slows in the slough
find1.cue: Mark the three places where moving water slows down and drops its mud.
find1.why: Moving water can carry tiny grains of mud. When it slows down, it cannot hold them any longer, so the grains settle to the bottom. Water slows among the marsh plants, on the inside of a channel bend and where a channel spreads onto flat ground. Those are the places where new mud builds up.
items: Stems slow the water, and mud drops.
the inside of the channel bend
Slow water on the inside leaves mud.
decoy: Useful for visitors, but water does not slow there.

select1.title: Read the tide board with the crew
select1.cue: Point to the tide board and say whether the tide is rising or falling.
select1.why: Everything in a tidal marsh follows the tide. The crew reads the tide board before every job so they know how long they have before the water returns. Reading it first is a safety habit, and it also tells you whether the water is bringing mud in or carrying it out.
select1.label: Tide board read

seq.title: Put the tide tray test in order
seq.cue: Stir in the mud, run slow water, look, then run fast water with the same mud.
seq.why: A fair test changes only one thing. You mix the same mud into the water each time and change only the speed. Running slow water first and fast water second, and looking closely after each, shows how speed decides where the mud settles. Looking closely after each run, before changing anything, is what keeps the two results apart.
seq.oon: Out of order. Stir in the mud first, then run the slow water.
items: stir the same scoop of mud into the water
run the water slowly across the tray
run the same muddy water fast

turn.title: Set the tray's water speed
turn.cue: Turn the pump dial to the slow setting for the first run.
turn.why: The pump dial controls how fast the water moves across the tray. Setting it exactly on slow for the first run gives you a clear starting point. Then you can turn it to fast for the second run and know that speed is the only thing that changed.
turn.label: Water speed

gauge.title: Read the mud layer in the tray
gauge.cue: Commit when the marker sits at the top of the new mud layer.
gauge.why: The new layer shows how much mud dropped out of the water. Reading its top against the tray's scale lets you compare the slow and fast runs fairly. Slow water usually leaves the thicker layer, which is why calm marsh water builds up new ground.
gauge.label: Mud layer
gauge.miss: Not at the top of the layer. Read where the new mud stops.

hold.title: Hold the plant strip in the tray
hold.cue: Hold the model plant strip in place until the water settles.
hold.why: The plant strip stands for the marsh grass. If it lifts, the water runs under it and the test changes. Holding it steady lets you see how stems slow the water and make mud settle right among them, just as it does in a real marsh. Keeping the strip in place means the slow and fast runs both meet the same model plants.
hold.brk: The strip lifted before the water settled. Hold it in place again.
hold.label: Hold the plant strip

drag.title: Place a crew mat on the model mud
drag.cue: Drag the wide mat onto the soft mud beside the model channel.
drag.why: Crews working on soft mud lay down wide mats to spread their weight, the way snowshoes work on snow. A mat keeps people and small machines from sinking and protects the mud and plants underneath. Placing it before anyone steps there is how the crew keeps the job steady.
drag.label: Crew mat
drag.miss: Not on the soft mud yet. Place the mat where the crew will stand.

find2.title: Spot how the crew helps mud build up
find2.cue: Look across the slough and mark each part of the crew's work.
find2.why: Restoration crews help the tide bring mud where the marsh needs it. They open channels so tides can reach the marsh, lower old banks so water spreads out, and reuse dug mud to raise low spots. Each job helps the marsh gain height with the help of the water itself.
items: Tides can reach the marsh again.
Water spreads out and slows down.
a pile of dug mud being reused
Low spots get raised with it.
decoy: It brings tools, but it is not part of the mud work.

select2.title: Say where the mud settled
select2.cue: Choose the sentence that says what your two runs showed.
select2.why: Your two runs used the same mud but different speeds. More mud settled when the water was slow. A good answer says that slow water drops more mud, which is why calm marshes build up. It uses your layer readings as the evidence. A careful conclusion sticks to the evidence in the table and leaves out guesses.
select2.label: State the result

track.title: Follow a cloud of mud across the tray
track.cue: Keep the marker on the cloud of mud as it drifts and settles.
track.why: Following one cloud of mud shows the process as it happens. It drifts with the water, spreads out among the plants and slowly sinks to the bottom. Seeing it settle helps you explain why marshes need muddy water, not only clear water. In the real slough, each tide brings a new cloud of fine mud into the marsh.
track.brk: The marker lost the mud cloud. Find it again and follow it until it settles.
track.label: Mud cloud followed

record.title: Record both runs side by side
record.cue: Write the layer reading for the slow run and the fast run in a table.
record.why: Two columns make the difference easy to see and easy to check. Anyone reading your table can see what changed and what stayed the same. Scientists who study the Bay's mud keep careful records like this so they can plan where marshes can grow.
record.label: Tray record

share.title: Compare with another group
share.cue: Put your table next to another group's and look for the same pattern.
share.why: If another group also finds that slow water drops more mud, the result is stronger. Comparing results is how scientists build confidence in an idea. Crews and scientists share findings about moving mud so that restoration plans work with the water.
share.label: Compare with a group

checkin.title: Check in before the tide turns
checkin.cue: Where does moving water drop its mud? Why does a marsh need it?
checkin.why: The crew finishes before the tide turns, and the class checks its ideas in time too. Each learner says where mud settles and why the marsh needs it. If anyone thinks the mud is only dirt, the group sorts it out now. Understanding moving mud helps everyone see a marsh as a living place that grows with each tide.
checkin.label: End-of-lesson check-in

interrupts.label: Move back up the firm path
interrupts.alert: The crew lead calls that the tide has turned and water is creeping up the channel.
interrupts.cue: Move back up the firm path with the crew and watch from higher ground.
interrupts.why: A rising tide can cover low mud quickly. Moving up the firm path early keeps everyone dry and steady. The crew plans every job to finish before the tide returns and never waits until the water arrives.
interrupts.miss: The class stayed by the channel edge, and the crew lead had to call everyone back up as the water reached the path.
interrupts.wrong: That keeps you low by the channel. Move up the firm path. Choose the response that deals with it now.
interrupts.done: Class on higher ground, the tide coming in. The lesson carries on.

interrupts.label: Say why the crew uses mats
interrupts.alert: The crew lead asks why the crew stands on wide mats.
interrupts.cue: Say the mats spread weight so people and machines do not sink.
interrupts.why: Knowing about the mats shows you understand soft ground. A wide mat spreads weight over more mud, so nobody sinks. It also protects the marsh plants below.
interrupts.miss: You could not say why the crew uses mats, and the crew lead had to explain before the class could go on.
interrupts.wrong: That does not explain the mats. Say what they do to weight. Choose the response that deals with it now.
interrupts.done: Mats explained. The lesson carries on.

guide.hazard: Stop. Firm path and tide board first.

lateRecord: The tray record is written once both runs are done — nothing to record yet.
lateCheckin: The check-in comes at the very end of the lesson.
